heading: Scintillator and Single Photon Sensor
content: The detector uses a 5 × 5 × 1 cm³ slab of organic plastic scintillator, rated to yield approximately 10,000 photons/MeV of deposited energy. A portion of these photons reach a photosensor, an OnSemiconductor MicroFC SiPM with a 6 mm × 6 mm active area, operated at 30 V reverse bias.

heading: Digital Electronics
content: At the heart of the detector’s digital system is the Raspberry Pi Pico (RPi), a dual-core MCU operating at 133 MHz. While one core handles time-critical data acquisition tasks, the other manages peripheral communication, like the OLED display, microSD card, and environmental sensors. The separation of these tasks significantly reduces dead time.

heading: Environmental Sensors
content: Additional digital peripherals, such as a temperature and pressure sensor (BMP280), and an accelerometer and gyroscope (MPU-6050), provide additional information to help with data analysis.

heading: Powering
content: The detector itself can be powered through a USB port on a computer, using a small battery, power bank, a mobile phone, or through the coincidence cable. A single detector consumes 0.5 W. For context, a commonly available 5,000 mAh power bank was measured to power two detectors for 18 hours.
